newsitem.title: UK: Europe copper demand muted, off-grade metal tight.
newsitem.headline: Europe copper demand muted, off-grade metal tight.

text.p: Underlying demand for copper in Europe has been slow so far in September, but a prolonged period of low scrap supplies has meant Russian metal availability is reduced to virtually nothing, industry sources said.
Merchants and consumers also welcomed the advent of a contango in the nearby London Metal Exchange (LME) spread structure, arguing it will spur stock rebuilding and offtake.
"Underlying business is reasonable. But it is not running away because Europe is so sluggish," said one merchant.
Conditions in the U.S. and Asia are healthier, he added.
"There is no sign of a pick-up as far as we are concerned," said a major European consumer.

Some physical traders took heart from the fact that Russian copper was virtually unobtainable. The shortage of scrap caused by the sharp fall in copper prices has boosted demand for Russian off-grade material considerably, they explained.
"Standard copper has gone in Europe, snapped up as a substitute for scrap shortages," said a trader.
Discounts for Russian copper have almost vanished, reflecting tightness. Traders said differentials were notional, but levels of $10 below to flat to LME cash were being quoted.
This compares with $50 to $70 a tonne below two weeks ago.
One trader said the off-grade shortage should provide a platform for better cathode demand.
"This is a good foundation for potential enquiries for LME cathodes," he said.
But another said the vanishing discounts were more likely to dampen demand.
"This would have helped the cathode market if demand in Europe was better. But I think what will happen is those players who were taking material when it was cheap will now stop doing so," he said.
"But there will obviously be some substitution," he added.
LME stocks fell slightly in September from 275,775 tonnes to 265,450 tonnes as of September 19.
Traders said some of the material was destined for the Far East. Rumours circulated that Chinese interest in Rotterdam warrants emerged recently.
"You can ship as little as 1,000 to 2,000 tonnes out to the Far East and make it work," said one trader. "Copper is cheaper in Europe than it is in the U.S."
There was also swapping, with local European deliveries being met out of LME warehouses while copper from producers was diverted to the more bouyant Far Eastern market.

"Copper which should have been destined for Europe is going to Asia instead," said a producer, adding that this was one reason why premiums in some Italian locations had edged up. There was also talk of merchant stock-building to take advantage of cash discounts to forward rates.
"Merchants' stockholding function is again in play. This hasn't happened the whole time that Sumitomo was squeezing the market," one merchant said.
But despite the shortage of off-grade material and rising warrant demand, some consumers said LME-deliverable copper was still freely available.
"I have been offered plenty of material in-warehouse and on a cif basis," said a consumer.
